thread.title: U.S. Tech Stocks Show Clear Signs Of Irrational Behavior

author: Kenra Investors
title: U.S. Tech Stocks Show Clear Signs Of Irrational Behavior
text:
What we have seen in the past few weeks in the tech sector are unequivocal signs of irrational behavior starting to spread. Let’s forget about the Nasdaq reaching new highs, which doesn’t tell us much per se, and let’s focus on how single stocks have behaved recently.
I want to start with Dropbox ( DBX ), whose shares surged 14% on Thursday and are up 8% Friday on basically no news. The only potential driver of the increase could be the announcement (earlier this week), that the company is expanding the capacity of its Magic Pocket infrastructure project with the mass deployment of Shingled Magnetic Recording (SMR) drive technology, which could bring some savings. If that was the news, I wonder why the stock didn't react to it before. Moreover, the company didn't disclose the amount of potential cost savings coming from the measure.
Somebody said there might be something else moving the stock, such as a potential acquisition. In the past, Dropbox has been pegged as an acquisition target by a few analysts. For example, Piper Jaffray mentioned Apple ( AAPL ), Salesforce ( CRM ), Cisco ( CSCO ), Alphabet ( GOOG ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) as companies with the potential to buy Dropbox. I am very skeptical about a potential acquisition moving the stock for two main reasons:
From a strategic perspective, it doesn’t make any sense for any of the tech giants mentioned above to spend over $12 billion to buy a company whose products are basically commoditized and can be easily replicated without huge investments. Many of these players are already offering cloud storage and file-sharing services as free features of their larger software products or operating systems. No rumors of an acquisition started to spread in the past few days. If somebody actually knows anything and is buying, good luck with the SEC. The market is valuing Dropbox 30% above the levels of last week, and the only visible reason is a late reaction to the possibility to see an uncertain amount of cost savings from the deployment of SMR Technology.
The second absurd phenomenon involves Adyen’s ( ADYEN ) IPO, a Dutch payment processor that competes against PayPal ( PYPL ) and the likes. If you don’t know it, it’s the payment processor that "stole" the eBay ( EBAY ) business from PayPal. The stock surged 90% on its first day. There is no way a stock at the IPO can be so mispriced unless you actually believe Adyen’s institutional investors want to give us a beautiful gift.
Netflix ( NFLX ), one of Wall Street’s growth darling, continues to reach new highs almost on a weekly basis and is very close to $400, while it was trading in the $200 area just 6 months ago. It’s surely a wonderful growth story if we look at revenue and subscribers, but the 30% rally that occurred between May and June is not backed by any evident catalyst. Looking at alternative datasets, it’s actually very likely that the users’ growth rate will decrease in the short-term. Let’s give a look at Google Trends. In the chart below, I plotted a 13-week moving average of the Y/Y variation in searches for “Netflix” on Google. In other words, it’s a chart that tells us how much searches have grown in the past three months over the same period last year. As you can see, the growth rate is declining significantly, while shares have skyrocketed.
Source: sentieo.com
There was basically no news supporting the rally if we exclude a few upgrades that certainly don’t justify such a solid increase in the stock price. One example is the recent upgrade from Goldman Sachs, which cited an inflection point where the company will turn cash flow positive . Goldman Sachs’ analyst wrote: "2018 will be the peak negative free cash flow year for Netflix, with revenue growth beginning to outpace content spend growth next year". Anybody who is buying NFLX at these levels on such a weak argument has basically misunderstood what has happened to the stock so far. In the past twelve months, Netflix reported over $1.8 billion in negative free cash flow, and $671 million of net income on paper. The stock trades at over 260x LTM EPS and 13.4x sales. Somebody should explain Goldman Sachs’ analysts that the market couldn’t care less about Netflix’s free cash flow. The reality is that, while fundamental improvements in users growth and revenue supported the previous run-ups, there are no fundamental improvements that justify Netflix’s rally in the past month. On the other side, the market has completely ignored a series of negative signs that could indicate mounting competitive pressures on Netflix's business. In a previous article , I pointed out two of the most important negative factors that could affect Netflix's business in the medium term:
Increasing competition from Disney ( DIS ), which is going to launch a streaming service next year and pull out all its Disney, Marvel, Pixar, Lucasfilm and, if they buy it, Fox content from Netflix to make it exclusive to its streaming service; The fall of net neutrality, which opens a new world of potential competitive possibilities in the streaming industry. Without net neutrality in place, internet service providers such as Comcast ( CMCSA ) and Charter Communications ( CHTR ) can prevent users from accessing some websites or decide to provide slower speeds for certain service/applications. In theory, they may even redirect users from one website to another. This means that a company like Comcast may simply block Netflix and damage it permanently if it's convenient for them. They may also make it extremely slow or intermittent, with an exponential rise in consumers’ frustration. Although I am personally against the measure, I can’t ignore the disruptive effect it would have on the streaming business. For all those companies offering both internet services and cable-TV, I think this kind of retaliation will probably become a standard. There is no way this can have a neutral effect on Netflix. Even if I assume a company like Comcast will not try to block Netflix, we can’t exclude it may try to collect higher fees from the access to the streaming service (from users or directly from Netflix). The market decided to ignore those factors and it could make sense when subscribers' growth was accelerating, but it's doing it again now as the new highs show the market has completely ignored the approval of the merger between AT&T ( T ) and Time Warner ( TWX ) and Comcast's consequent bid on Fox ( FOXA )'s assets. The approval of the AT&T/Time Warner merger paves the way to a potential series of mergers that will increase consolidation in the media industry, which will result in Netflix competing against even bigger players. We have seen what would be the effects in terms of competitive pressures if Disney managed to buy Fox's assets. A merger with Comcast may have the same effect, as the telecom conglomerate would own 60% of competing platform Hulu, and could consider a Disney-like move to make its content (which will include Fox productions as well) exclusive to its streaming platforms. The consolidation in the industry, which will continue for sure, and the effects it could have on Netflix, were completely ignored by the market.
Then we have Snap ( SNAP ), which is simply amazing. The stock rose almost 30% on no news other than Citron’s bullish case. Conversely, the market doesn’t seem to care much about Citron’s short thesis on Netflix . Strange, considering that Citron is mainly famous for its short picks. Regarding SNAP, I have to say I rarely disagree with Citron but this time I can’t avoid pointing out how their bullish case completely ignores aspects such as profitability, monetization and the declining users’ growth (compared with Instagram’s strong momentum), but that’s not the main point. The main point is that the market is reacting to information with a high selectivity, ignoring bad news and over-reacting to good news. For example, investors are completely ignoring Snapchat’s slowing users growth. According to data from Sensor Tower, Snapchat’s DAU declined 22% in the first two months of the second quarter, while Instagram’s DAU’s continued to grow at healthy rates. The market also ignored the fact that Instagram is replicating another Snapchat feature – Snap Discover.
What’s the best example of an irrational behavior of a market that reacts only to good news?
